title: Leaving work
hookLine: a clear end to the workday: in Genesis, God looks back, calls it very good, and ends the work
tomorrow: can sweeping a room turn it into gold?

cards: The laptop is closed. Then the phone buzzes at eleven, and the workday quietly starts again. Genesis tells how a stretch of work ends.
After six days of making light and sea, plants, animals and people, God looks at it all: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good."
Then the text slows down: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made."

teach.h: FIRST A LOOK BACK: VERY GOOD.
teach.b: Notice the order. First, a look back. All through the chapter the text pauses to say what's made is good, and at the end, very good.
Then, an ending on purpose. The work doesn't fizzle out at midnight; it's ended. And the word good comes before the word rested.
The rest isn't a collapse at the end of the week. It follows a verdict. Jews built a whole day on that ending.

teach.h: SIX DAYS OF WORK, THEN SHABBAT.
teach.b: The commandments in Exodus point straight back to this chapter: "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work," and the seventh is the sabbath, for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and rested.
That's Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, which begins at sundown on Friday. Christians hear the same chapter behind their own day of rest.
The teaching for a workday is the shape of it: look at what you did, call it good, or good enough, and end it on purpose. Not because the list is empty. Lists are never empty.

teach.h: THE ENDING IS PART OF THE WORK.
teach.b: Because the ending is part of the work.
You can hear it in the text's rhythm: made, saw, good, ended, rested.

how: Jews end each week's work with Shabbat, from Friday sundown, and Christians keep a day of rest; both point back to Genesis, where God looks at the work, calls it very good, and ends it.

o: quitting a job to find one that feels better
a set end to the workday, chosen and kept
logging off the minute your manager logs off

games.q: how the work ends: tap the pairs.
p: what God saw when he looked back
the Jewish day of rest, from Friday sundown

s: a workday is over when the to-do list is empty
in Genesis the work ends with a look back and a decision to end it.
the commandment ties the week's rest to the creation story
for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and rested the seventh.
Genesis says God stopped because he was worn out
the text says he ended his work and rested. it doesn't say he was tired.

games.q: your friend answers clients from bed every night 'because there's always more.' what does the Genesis pattern suggest?
o: pick an end: look back at the day, call it good enough, and stop on purpose.
work until the inbox is empty; that's when work is honestly finished.
rest only on weekends; weekday nights belong to the job.
games.why: in Genesis the ending is a choice made after a look back: very good, then ended.

practice: Put both hands flat on a table or desk and feel its surface under your palms. Walk back through today's work, one piece at a time, and say quietly at the end of each: good.
Then lift your hands off the table, slowly, and let them rest in your lap.

wordCard.voice: Leaving work: a clear end to the workday, looked back on and set down on purpose, the way Genesis ends the six days.

orig.note: Hebrew: the Sabbath, the day Jews keep each week as the end of the week's work.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: done, seen and called good and set down for today. The workday's over.
